clue.text: These army jumpers ride up!

parts.note: jumpers here are not sweaters creeping up the body but soldiers who leap from aircraft and ride the air currents

explanation.surface: A complaint that these army-issue sweaters keep creeping up the wearer's back.
explanation.walkthrough: Jumpers is the British word for sweaters, which notoriously ride up; the army's own jumpers are men who leap from planes.
explanation.definitionFit: Airborne soldiers who jump by parachute into battle are exactly the army's jumpers.

clue.text: University in capital dock-area that is approved

indicators.note: the university letter is placed inside the dock district

parts.note: Poplar is a district of London's Docklands

explanation.surface: A university set up in a London docklands area wins approval.
explanation.walkthrough: Poplar is an East London district by the old docks.
explanation.definitionFit: Something well liked and widely favoured is popular.

clue.text: Cane the palm?

explanation.surface: A question whether to beat someone across the palm of the hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Rattan (also spelt ratan) is a climbing palm whose stems make cane furniture and sticks.

clue.text: Where to see beginning and end of the rainbow?

definitions.text: Where to see beginning and end of the rainbow?

parts.words: Where to see beginning and end of the rainbow?
parts.note: the rainbow is a fish species, and its whole life from hatching to harvest is spent at one breeding site

explanation.surface: Asking where one might view both ends of a rainbow in the sky.
explanation.walkthrough: The rainbow is not in the sky: rainbow trout are bred and raised to market on such farms.
explanation.definitionFit: A fish farm raising rainbow trout sees them from spawn to slaughter.

clue.text: Heartless Humpty-Dumptyish poet

indicators.note: heartless means the central letter of the word is removed

parts.note: Humpty Dumpty is an egg in the nursery rhyme, so egg-shaped, ovoid

explanation.surface: A poet who is cruel and resembles Humpty Dumpty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heartless' removes the middle O of OVOID.
explanation.definitionFit: Ovid was the Roman author of the Metamorphoses.

clue.text: Composer, violinist and heathen in one

parts.note: a pagan is a heathen
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A musician described as a composer, a fiddler and an unbeliever all at once.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in one' looks like 'combined', but gives IN and I.
explanation.definitionFit: Niccolò Paganini was the Italian virtuoso fiddler who also wrote music.

clue.text: Becoming fit

explanation.surface: Getting into shape.
explanation.definitionFit: Becoming means proper or fitting, as is right; fit means well, as in right as rain.

clue.text: Small cars go with lots of revs

parts.note: Minis are small British cars
a go is an attempt, a try

explanation.surface: Little cars accompanied by plenty of engine revving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revs' is not engine speed but Reverends, clergy collectively.
explanation.definitionFit: The clergy as a body form the ministry.

clue.text: Camp for a period in filthy place

indicators.note: the period is put inside the filthy place

parts.note: a sty, where pigs live, is a filthy place
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: Camping for a while somewhere squalid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Camp' is not a tent site but the adjective meaning theatrical.
explanation.definitionFit: Camp means exaggerated and theatrical in manner.

clue.text: For underground exploration, take river bearing in Scotland

parts.note: the Po is the great river of northern Italy
thole is a Scots verb meaning to bear or endure, so tholing is bearing

explanation.surface: Advice to a caver to take a river route while carrying something in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: THOLE (to endure) survives in Scots and northern English dialect.
explanation.definitionFit: Caving down shafts and sinkholes is the hobby of exploring underground passages.

clue.text: Dressing applied to George's head in a flash

indicators.note: the head of the name George is its opening letter

parts.note: lint is a soft fabric used to dress wounds

explanation.surface: Someone puts a bandage on George's head very quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a flash' looks like 'quickly', but 'flash' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A glint is a brief sparkle or gleam of light.

clue.text: Woolly article in past

indicators.note: the article is set inside the word for past

parts.note: late means former, of the past
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A woolly garment from bygone days.
explanation.definitionFit: Lanate is a botanical term for covered in fine hairs like fleece.

clue.text: What can happen in a New York night out?

indicators.note: out signals that these letters are put out of order

explanation.surface: Wondering what might occur during a night out on the town in New York.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' seems to belong with 'night out', but it is the anagram signal, making NYTHING.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying goes that on a wild evening any event at all can happen.

clue.text: Fun for students to label a scruffy person

parts.note: a rag is a British university students' charity carnival of pranks and fun
to bag is to claim or mark something as one's own, tagging it

explanation.surface: Student high jinks used as an excuse to stick a label on a shabby individual.
explanation.walkthrough: RAG week is a British student fundraising tradition.
explanation.definitionFit: A ragbag is slang for an untidily dressed, slovenly individual.

clue.text: Looking only briefly, girl's first to go over boys' school

indicators.note: in a down entry, going over means being placed above the next piece
first takes just the opening letter of the word girl

parts.note: Lancing College is an English public school, formerly for boys

explanation.surface: A girl glancing over a boys' school.
explanation.walkthrough: Lancing is a public school in Sussex.
explanation.definitionFit: Glancing means taking a quick look.

clue.text: Valiant after dark, say

indicators.note: say tells us the word for after dark is to be spoken, giving another spelling

parts.note: nightly means happening at night

explanation.surface: Someone is described as brave once night falls.
explanation.definitionFit: Chivalrous and brave, as a knight of romance should be.

clue.text: Take a fare that's within reach

parts.note: to get is to take
the table one keeps is the food served, one's fare

explanation.surface: Ordering a meal that is close at hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Get-at-able is informal for accessible, reachable.

clue.text: The saloon may be battered but the wares are given endless care

parts.note: a shop's stock is its wares

indicators.note: endless means the final letter of the word care is dropped

explanation.surface: A bar may be wrecked while its goods are looked after with endless care.
explanation.walkthrough: The saloon is a car, not a bar: stock-car racing is a sport of battered saloons.
explanation.definitionFit: Stock car racing uses ordinary saloon cars that get dented and battered.

clue.text: Tea amply stirred for companion

indicators.note: stirred, as of a cup of tea, means the letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: Someone stirs a generous cup of tea for a friend.
explanation.definitionFit: A playmate is a friend or partner one plays with.

clue.text: Kind of medicine for person under treatment losing heart?

indicators.note: losing heart means the central letter of the word is removed

parts.note: a patient is someone receiving medical treatment

explanation.surface: A drug for someone being treated who has lost courage.
explanation.definitionFit: Patent medicines are proprietary remedies sold over the counter.

clue.text: Put off retirement and settle in a more northerly place

definitions.text: settle in a more northerly place

explanation.surface: Someone delays retiring and moves house up north.
explanation.definitionFit: To not go to bed is to put off retiring for the night; to remain up north is to settle in the north.

clue.text: Jam being served for the exercise

parts.note: to jam is to press tightly
food that is up is ready and being served

explanation.surface: Jam being dished up for some exercise.
explanation.definitionFit: A press-up is a gym movement lifting the body by the arms.

clue.text: The prices it gives, of course, are for the second annex

definitions.text: The prices it gives, of course

parts.note: a tick is a moment, a second
to tack is to attach or annex

explanation.surface: A puzzling statement about prices relating to a second annex of a building.
explanation.walkthrough: Tick-tack is the hand-signalling bookmakers use on British racecourses to pass on betting odds; 'course' means racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: Bookmakers' sign language relays the betting odds around a racecourse.

clue.text: Greek character, the first in Tartarus suffering heat

indicators.note: the first in Tartarus is its opening letter
suffering suggests the letters of heat are tormented out of order

explanation.surface: A Greek figure, the first to suffer the heat in the Underworld.
explanation.walkthrough: Tartarus is the pit of torment in Greek myth, which suits 'suffering' as the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Theta is the eighth letter of the Greek alphabet.

clue.text: Key fastener of wire

explanation.surface: A key fastener made of wire.
explanation.definitionFit: A staple diet is a main or principal one; a staple is also a bent wire clip for fixing paper.

clue.text: Drink made him a wife-beater

explanation.surface: Alcohol turned a man violent towards his spouse.
explanation.definitionFit: Punch is a mixed fruit drink; Mr Punch in the Punch and Judy puppet show beats his wife Judy.

clue.text: Aggressor can catch the sea-whale

indicators.note: the words aggressor can catch, or hold, the answer within them

explanation.surface: An aggressor can catch the sea-whale.
explanation.definitionFit: The killer whale is the grampus or orca.

clue.text: Name formerly used for the present occasion

parts.note: once means at a former time

explanation.surface: A name that was used in the past is now used just for today.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for the nonce' means for the time being.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonce word is coined for one particular occasion only.

clue.text: Wild attendants freed Byron's cat

indicators.note: freed suggests the letters are let loose and rearranged

parts.note: the possessive here counts its S as a letter of the fodder

explanation.surface: Wild servants let the poet Byron's cat go.
explanation.definitionFit: Corybants were frenzied priests and followers of the goddess Cybele.

clue.text: Long, golden vessel in Masefield's office?

parts.note: aureate means golden
a ship is a sea-going vessel

explanation.surface: A long golden boat appears in the poet Masefield's office.
explanation.walkthrough: John Masefield was Britain's Poet Laureate from 1930 to 1967.
explanation.definitionFit: The post of Poet Laureate was the role Masefield held for decades.
